summary: The premier food security staple of Malawi, grown by over 90% of smallholders.
uses: Nsima, mgaiwa, and ufa oyera household flour
Fresh roasted and boiled green maize
Livestock and poultry feed from yellow maize, bran (gaga) and stover
field: Select certified hybrid or OPV variety matching your district's rainfall duration (Early: SC 403, Kanyani; Medium: SC 627, Peacock 10; Late: SC 719).
Construct 75cm ridges with tied ridges every 2m to capture rainfall.
Plant 1 seed per station at 25cm spacing within 48 hours of effective rainfall (≥25mm).
Apply 4 bags/ha of 23:10:5+6S basal fertiliser within 7 days of emergence.
Top-dress with 4 bags/ha of Urea at knee-height (21-28 days after planting).
Dry harvested cobs until grain moisture is below 13.5% before storage in PICS bags.
watch: Scout weekly for Fall Armyworm (FAW) funnels, African maize stalk borer, Grey Leaf Spot, and larger grain weevils in storage.
soilRequirements: Deep, well-drained sandy-loam or clay-loam soils. pH 5.5 – 7.0. Sensitive to waterlogging.
fertiliserRecommendations: Basal: 200 kg/ha 23:10:5+6S. Top-dress: 200 kg/ha Urea in moist soil. Incorporate 5–10 tonnes/ha well-rotted manure.
ecologicalSuitability: All districts across Malawi; medium plateau (Lilongwe, Kasungu) provides optimum yields.

summary: High-value legume grown for food nutrition, edible oil extraction, confectionery export, and soil nitrogen enrichment.
uses: Household relish, peanut butter, and children's porridge supplement
Commercial sale to agro-processors and confectionery export markets
Haulms (zitsamba) used as nutrient-dense dry-season cattle and goat fodder
field: Choose recommended seed: CG7 (Virginia runner for confectionery), Chalimbana 2005, or Nsinjiro.
Plant on broad 75cm ridges, double rows per ridge, 15cm between stations, 1 seed per hole.
Do NOT weed or hoe after pegging begins to avoid severing delicate developing pods.
Apply agricultural gypsum at flowering (200 kg/ha) to supply calcium and prevent 'pops' (empty shells).
Lift crop promptly when 70% of inner shells display dark brown veining.
Dry pods on raised slatted racks (Mandala racks) away from soil moisture to prevent Aspergillus aflatoxins.
watch: Groundnut rosette disease (spread by aphids in sparse stands), leaf spots (Cercospora), and damp post-harvest aflatoxin contamination.
soilRequirements: Light, friable, loose sandy loams allowing easy peg entry and clean pod lifting. pH 5.8 – 6.5.
fertiliserRecommendations: Incorporate single superphosphate (SSP) or gypsum. High nitrogen fertilisers are not recommended as plants fix their own N.
plantingWindow: Late November to Early December (plant early with first rains)
ecologicalSuitability: Medium altitude plains: Lilongwe, Mchinji, Kasungu, Dowa, Mzimba.

summary: Protein-dense commercial legume vital for human nutrition, vegetable oil pressing, and animal feed manufacturing.
uses: Soy milk, soy pieces, flour enrichment, and edible oil
High-protein poultry and dairy feed compounding
Soil nitrogen replenishment in cereal rotations
field: Source certified high-yielding varieties such as Tikolore, Makwacha, or Nasoko.
Inoculate seeds in the shade with Rhizobium bio-fertiliser inoculant slurry just before sowing.
Plant double rows on 75cm ridges, 5cm between seeds in continuous drill.
Ensure early weeding within the first 3 weeks; plants suppress weeds once canopy closes.
Harvest promptly when 90% of foliage has dropped and pods turn tan/brown and rattle.
Harvest early in the morning before midday heat to minimize shattering losses.
watch: Soybean rust (Phakopsora pachyrhizi), red leaf blotch, pod-shattering at maturity, and cutworms during seedling emergence.
soilRequirements: Well-aerated loams with moderate moisture capacity. pH 6.0 – 6.8. Sensitive to soil capping.
fertiliserRecommendations: Basal application of D-Compound or Superphosphate (100 kg/ha) alongside bacterial Rhizobium inoculation.
ecologicalSuitability: Central and Northern plateaus: Kasungu, Dowa, Ntchisi, Dedza, Mzimba.

summary: Major cash and staple cereal cultivated in flooded dambos, river plains, and managed irrigation schemes.
uses: Daily urban and rural table rice (prized for aroma)
Commercial sale to wholesale millers and regional export
Rice bran for livestock rations and rice husks for poultry bedding
field: Choose aromatic certified varieties: Kilombero, Faya, Nunkile, or ITA 312.
Establish raised nursery beds in November; water regularly and rogue off-types.
Puddle paddy field thoroughly to control weeds and create a soft mud layer.
Transplant 21-day-old seedlings (2-3 seedlings per hill) at 20cm x 20cm spacing.
Maintain 5-10cm standing water during vegetative and heading stages.
Top dress with Urea in 2 splits: 3 weeks after transplanting and at panicle initiation.
Drain paddy 10-14 days before harvest to allow uniform ripening.
watch: Rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae), stem borers, bird predation during milky grain stage, and late-season water shortages.
soilRequirements: Heavy clay, silty clay, or alluvial lowland soils with low permeability that retain standing water. pH 5.0 – 6.5.
fertiliserRecommendations: Basal: 150 kg/ha 23:10:5+6S at puddling. Top-dress: 150 kg/ha Urea split at early tillering and panicle initiation.
plantingWindow: Nursery in November; Transplanting December to January
ecologicalSuitability: Karonga, Salima, Nkhotakota, Machinga (Lake Chilwa basin), Shire Valley.

summary: Resilient drought-tolerant root staple, foundational to food security along Lake Malawi and growing industrial starch markets.
uses: Kondowole (cassava porridge staple in Nkhata Bay and Karonga)
Boiled fresh roots and sun-dried makaka slices
High-grade cassava flour (HQCF) for bakery blending and industrial paper/adhesive starch
field: Use certified disease-free stem cuttings of improved varieties: Sauti, Manyokola, Yizaso, or Chitembwere.
Cut mature stems into 25-30cm lengths containing 4-6 healthy buds.
Plant cuttings on ridges at 45-degree angle, 1m apart (10,000 plants/ha).
Keep field rigorously weed-free during the first 3-4 months until canopy closes.
Rogue out and burn any plants exhibiting yellow mosaic leaf distortion or vein clearing.
Harvest roots selectively from 9-12 months onward; process within 48 hours to avoid vascular browning.
watch: Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD), Cassava Brown Streak Disease (CBSD), cassava mealybug, and green mite.
soilRequirements: Deep, well-drained friable sandy loams. Tolerates low nutrient status but yields highest in aerated soils.
fertiliserRecommendations: Responds well to organic compost and potassium-rich ash. Moderate 23:10:5 applied at month 2 boosts commercial root bulking.
ecologicalSuitability: Lakeside belt (Nkhata Bay, Nkhotakota, Salima), Lower Shire, and Karonga.

summary: Fast-maturing, nutrient-rich root crop, especially orange-fleshed varieties that combat vitamin A deficiency.
uses: Boiled and roasted breakfast roots
Orange-fleshed purees for infant nutrition and baked goods
Tender young leaves (kholowa) cooked as nutritious relish
field: Procure clean terminal vine cuttings (30cm long) of high-yielding varieties: Zondeni (Orange-fleshed), Kaphulira, or Kenya.
Construct high mounds or continuous 75-90cm ridges to promote root expansion.
Plant vines at 30cm spacing, burying two-thirds of the cutting into moist soil.
Weed early and mound additional soil around vines at 4 weeks to prevent exposed roots.
Harvest at 3.5 to 5 months when roots reach marketable size before sweetpotato weevils penetrate.
watch: Sweetpotato weevil (Cylas spp.) tunneling into roots, Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD), and mole rats.
soilRequirements: Sandy loam soils with high organic matter. Heavy soils cause misshapen roots.
fertiliserRecommendations: High potassium promotes root bulking. Combine farmyard manure with moderate compound fertiliser.
plantingWindow: December to January (Rainfed); June to July (Dimba wetlands)
harvestWindow: April to May (Rainfed); September to October (Dimba)
ecologicalSuitability: Grown in all districts of Malawi; Dedza, Ntcheu, Thyolo, and Zomba are major producers.

summary: The highest-grossing fresh market vegetable across Malawi, grown in rainfed gardens and winter dimba wetlands.
uses: Essential daily relish cooking ingredient in every Malawian household
Commercial fresh supply to urban wholesale markets and supermarket chains
Tomato puree, paste, and sauce processing
field: Select high-performing varieties: Rodade, Heinz 1370, Roma VF, or indeterminate hybrids (Assila, Eden).
Raise seedlings in raised nursery beds under light grass thatch; drench with copper fungicide.
Transplant sturdy 4-week-old seedlings in the evening at 60cm x 50cm spacing.
Incorporate 1 shovelful of compost and 1 matchbox of Compound D per planting station.
Stake plants with sturdy wooden poles to keep foliage off moist soil and reduce fungal blight.
Side-dress with CAN fertiliser every 2-3 weeks from first flowering to encourage continuous fruit set.
watch: Tomato Late Blight (chikuku), Early Blight, Bacterial Wilt (ralstonia), Tuta Absoluta (leafminer), and red spider mites.
soilRequirements: Fertile, loose, well-drained loams rich in organic matter. pH 6.0 – 6.8. Avoid land previously cropped with potatoes or eggplants.
fertiliserRecommendations: Basal: Compound D or 23:10:5 (250 kg/ha). Top-dress: CAN or Urea (150 kg/ha in 3 split doses). Foliar calcium to prevent blossom end rot.
plantingWindow: Year-round under irrigation; primary winter crop sown March to May
harvestWindow: 75 to 90 days after transplanting (continuous picking for 6-8 weeks)
ecologicalSuitability: Dedza, Ntcheu, Thyolo, Zomba, Lilongwe rural, and lakeshore wetlands.

summary: Deep-rooting, drought-hardy legume vital to the farming systems and export economy of the Southern Region.
uses: Household fresh green peas and dry split grain (dal)
High-value export commodity to Indian subcontinent markets
Deep soil root aeration, leaf fall mulching, and dry woody stalks for household firewood
field: Select recommended varieties: Mthawajuni (medium duration), Kachangu, or Sauma.
Intercrop with maize by planting pigeon peas on the same ridge between maize stations.
Pigeon pea develops slowly while maize is growing, then bursts into full growth after maize harvest using residual deep soil moisture.
Weed alongside companion cereal; scout for pod-boring caterpillars at flowering stage.
Harvest mature pods and shell dry grain; store in sealed drums or treated bags to deter bruchid weevils.
watch: Fusarium wilt (chifukwa cha mtengo wofota), pod borers (Helicoverpa armigera), and storage bruchids (Callosobruchus).
soilRequirements: Adapts to poor, degraded, gravelly soils, but prefers deep well-drained loams. High drought tolerance.
fertiliserRecommendations: Rarely requires added fertiliser when intercropped with fertilized maize; deep taproot mines subsoil phosphorus.
plantingWindow: November to Mid-December (concurrent with maize planting)
harvestWindow: July to September (well after maize harvest)
ecologicalSuitability: Southern Highlands: Mulanje, Thyolo, Chiradzulu, Phalombe, Zomba, Machinga.

summary: Major cash crop in high-altitude zones of Malawi, commanding high market demand in urban centers.
uses: Boiled, mashed, and fried household food
Commercial supply to restaurant and chips (french fry) processors in Blantyre, Lilongwe and Mzuzu
field: Use certified disease-free seed tubers with sprouted chits of varieties: Rosita, Mpatsa, or Lady Rosetta.
Plant in well-loosened ridges 75cm apart, 30cm between tubers, 10-15cm deep.
Apply basal fertiliser (23:10:5+6S) at 300 kg/ha alongside well-rotted cattle manure.
Earthing up (banking) twice during vegetative growth is mandatory to prevent tuber greening.
Scout for late blight during cold mist and rainy spells; apply protective fungicides proactively.
De-haulm (cut tops) 10-14 days prior to harvest to toughen tuber skins for transport.
watch: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum), potato tuber moth, and aphids.
soilRequirements: Cool, loose, deep, acidic-to-neutral loamy soils (pH 5.0 – 6.0). Poor drainage leads to soft rot.
fertiliserRecommendations: Basal: 350 kg/ha 23:10:5+6S. Top-dress: 150 kg/ha CAN at first earthing up. Abundant manure.
plantingWindow: Rainfed: November – December; Winter Dimba: May – June
ecologicalSuitability: Highlands: Dedza, Ntcheu (Kirk Range), Dowa Hills, Viphya, Nyika, Misuku.

summary: Nutritious pulse grown as a primary source of vegetable protein and fast cash in upland districts.
uses: Daily household relish with nsima or rice
Fresh green pods and leaves used as vegetables
High-value trading grain across rural and urban markets
field: Choose certified bush or climbing varieties: Kholophethe (sugar bean), NUA45 (biofortified iron bean), or BCMV-resistant lines.
Plant on 75cm ridges at 10cm spacing (bush beans) or 20cm spacing with staking poles (climbing beans).
Weed early at 2 weeks; avoid field operations when leaves are wet to prevent spreading bacterial blights.
Harvest promptly when pods turn yellow-brown; dry on tarpaulins and thresh gently to avoid seed coat cracking.
watch: Bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), anthracnose, angular leaf spot, bean stem maggot, and storage weevils.
soilRequirements: Well-drained fertile loams rich in organic matter. pH 6.0 – 6.8. Sensitive to acid soils with high aluminum.
fertiliserRecommendations: Apply single superphosphate (SSP) or 100 kg/ha 23:10:5 at planting. Nitrogen application should be limited.
plantingWindow: First season: December; Second season (uplands): February to March; Dimba: May to June
ecologicalSuitability: Mid to high elevation: Dedza, Ntcheu, Dowa, Ntchisi, Mzimba, Rumphi, Chitipa.

summary: Major industrial cash crop for smallholders in hot lowland river basins, feeding domestic textile ginning and export.
uses: Raw seed cotton for national ginning and lint export
Cottonseed oil processing for edible oils and soap manufacturing
Cottonseed cake for high-protein livestock feed
field: Plant certified hybrid or open-pollinated seed treated against early seedling pests.
Sow on 75-90cm ridges, 30cm between stations with 2-3 seeds per hole, thinning to 1 plant at 3 weeks.
Scout fields weekly from squaring for bollworms (American, Red, and Spiny) using pegboards.
Apply targeted scouting-based sprays rather than calendar spraying to protect beneficial predatory insects.
Harvest seed cotton in clean cotton-picking bags; separate clean white Grade A locks from stained Grade B locks.
watch: African bollworm, red bollworm, cotton jassids, stainers (Dysdercus), and bacterial blight (black arm).
soilRequirements: Deep alluvial soils or heavy clay loams (Vertisols/Makande) with good moisture holding capacity. pH 6.0 – 7.5.
fertiliserRecommendations: Responds well to basal compound fertiliser and split nitrogen. Foliar boron prevents flower and boll abortion.
plantingWindow: Late November to Mid-December (with steady onset of rains)
ecologicalSuitability: Lower Shire Valley (Chikwawa, Nsanje), Salima, Karonga, and Balaka.

summary: Historic principal foreign-exchange earner of Malawi, produced as Burley and Flue-cured leaf.
uses: Commercial leaf sale through national auction floors (Lilongwe, Limbe, Mzuzu, Chinkhoma)
Foreign exchange generation and agricultural wage employment
field: Strictly source certified seed approved by the Agricultural Research and Extension Trust (ARET).
Sow nursery beds in August/September under grass thatch covers with prophylactic fungal drenching.
Transplant vigorous hardened seedlings in December onto 90-105cm ridges with Compound C (tobacco basal).
Top dress with CAN fertiliser; de-sucker and top flower heads at button stage to maximize leaf area expansion.
Harvest leaves progressively as they mature from bottom to top (primings to tips).
Cure Burley leaf in well-ventilated grass/thatch sheds with regulated humidity to prevent barn rot.
watch: Bushy top virus, brown spot (Alternaria), root-knot nematodes, aphids, and barn rot during humid curing.
soilRequirements: Deep sandy loams with good drainage and low chloride content. Waterlogging ruins leaf quality.
fertiliserRecommendations: Compound C (6:15:12) or specific ARET basal blends at 350 kg/ha. Top dress with CAN. Avoid muriate of potash.
plantingWindow: Seedbed: August – September; Field Transplanting: December
ecologicalSuitability: Kasungu, Lilongwe, Mchinji, Dowa, Rumphi, Mzimba.

summary: Perennial estate and smallholder cash crop grown in the high-rainfall slopes of Southern and Northern Malawi.
uses: Black tea manufacture for domestic consumption and global export auctions
Specialty green and artisanal estate teas
field: Propagated from vegetatively cloned cuttings (PC series from Tea Research Foundation of Central Africa - TRFCA).
Establish contour terraces and vetiver grass hedgerows on steep slopes to arrest erosion.
Maintain a dense plucking table by regular pruning cycles every 3-4 years.
Pluck 'two leaves and a bud' every 7 to 10 days during the peak wet season.
Transport plucked green leaf swiftly to processing factories in ventilated woven baskets.
watch: Helopeltis (tea mosquito bug), red spider mite, carpenter moth, and drought stress during hot dry spells.
soilRequirements: Deep, strongly acidic soils (pH 4.5 – 5.5) with no free calcium or hardpans. High organic matter.
fertiliserRecommendations: High-nitrogen specialized NPK blends (e.g. 25:5:5) applied during active flush periods.
plantingWindow: Field planting of nursery stumps in December – January
harvestWindow: Peak plucking: November to May; year-round under irrigation
ecologicalSuitability: Mulanje, Thyolo, and Nkhatabay (high rainfall >1200mm and cool misty climate).

summary: Specialty high-altitude Arabica crop celebrated internationally for its rich body, acidity, and floral aroma.
uses: Specialty single-origin washed Arabica coffee for export
Local roasting and coffee shop retail
field: Grow proven Arabica cultivars (Catimor, Geisha, SL28) raised in shade nurseries.
Plant on contour terraces spaced 2.5m x 1.5m under agroforestry shade trees (Albizia, Grevillea).
Mulch root zones generously with grass and banana leaves to preserve soil moisture.
Hand-pick exclusively deep red ripe cherries; pulp and wet-ferment on the same day.
Sun-dry washed parchment coffee on raised African drying beds until 11% moisture.
watch: Coffee Berry Disease (CBD), Coffee Leaf Rust (Hemileia vastatrix), white stem borer, and antestia bugs.
soilRequirements: Deep volcanic or well-weathered upland loams, rich in humus, with excellent subsoil drainage. pH 5.0 – 6.0.
fertiliserRecommendations: Compound fertiliser supplemented with manure and potassium sulfate. Foliar zinc and boron.
plantingWindow: Transplanting at start of steady rains in December
harvestWindow: May to August (Cherry picking and wet processing)
ecologicalSuitability: Highlands >1200m: Misuku Hills (Chitipa), Rumphi, Viphya, and parts of Zomba/Mangochi plateaus.

summary: Hardy oilseed crop with strong drought resilience, high seed oil percentage, and short maturity period.
uses: Cold-pressed edible cooking oil for home and market sale
High-protein sunflower cake for poultry and livestock feed
Pollinator nectar support for honey beekeeping
field: Use improved open-pollinated or hybrid seed: Record, Super 400, or local selections.
Plant on 75cm ridges, 30cm between stations (1-2 seeds per hole, thin to 1).
Weed during the first 4 weeks; sunflower develops a dense shading canopy quickly.
Protect mature heads from bird damage during seed-fill stage.
Harvest when the back of flower heads turns golden yellow to brown and bracts dry.
watch: Bird damage, head rot (Sclerotinia), cutworms, and damping off in waterlogged basins.
soilRequirements: Adaptable to a wide range of soils; performs well even on marginal sandy loams. pH 6.0 – 7.5.
fertiliserRecommendations: Moderate basal 23:10:5+6S (100 kg/ha). Boron is essential to prevent hollow seeds.
ecologicalSuitability: Central and Northern districts: Kasungu, Mzimba, Dowa, Salima, Balaka.

summary: Fast-yielding green vegetables that provide daily vitamins and immediate cash flow for smallholder gardens.
uses: Daily staple vegetable relish accompanying nsima
Continuous daily market sales in urban and village trading centres
field: Sow certified seed of Mpiru (mustard greens), Rape, Covo, or Chinese Cabbage in nursery beds.
Transplant after 3-4 weeks onto raised beds enriched with decomposed compost.
Space plants 30cm x 30cm; water daily at ground level to keep leaves clean.
Harvest outer leaves progressively, allowing inner shoots to continue generating new foliage.
watch: Diamondback moth caterpillars (DBM), aphids, damping off, and black rot.
soilRequirements: Rich, moisture-retentive loams with high organic matter. pH 6.0 – 7.0.
fertiliserRecommendations: Heavy organic manure plus CAN side-dressings every 2 weeks after each major leaf picking.
plantingWindow: Year-round in dambo wetlands and irrigated home gardens
harvestWindow: Continuous picking from 4 weeks after transplanting for up to 3 months
ecologicalSuitability: Cultivated across all districts of Malawi.
